text: Hands-on lab: take an under-specified, trust-me-it-worked result and rebuild it into a fully reproducible package — tagged commit, lockfile, and experiment record — then actually attempt to reproduce it as if you were a colleague six months later.

This lesson covers assembling all three reproducibility layers for one real experiment in order, a reproduction fire drill pretending you're someone else rebuilding a past result from scratch, what a reproducibility failure actually looks like and how to diagnose which layer was missing, and a reusable checklist to run before reporting any quantum result.

Here's the starting point: a shared doc says the four-qubit GHZ fidelity check got 0.97, and the code is on the experiments branch somewhere. This sentence is missing every piece this chapter built — no commit, no environment snapshot, no seed, no shot count, no backend version. It is not reproducible, even in principle, as written.

Fix it in three steps. First, find the actual commit that produced the result and tag it, following lesson fourteen's convention. Second, lock and commit the environment, following lesson fifteen. Third, assemble and save the experiment record with both the simulator and transpiler seeds and the shot count, following lesson sixteen, and commit that file too.

Step four is the fire drill: clone the repository into a fresh directory, simulating a colleague with no context six months later, check out the tagged commit, resync the exact locked environment, and run the experiment script reading its parameters directly from the saved metadata file rather than requiring anyone to remember or re-type them. This either reproduces a statistically consistent result, checked against the original confidence level, or reveals exactly which recorded piece was wrong or missing.

If the fire drill's result is inconsistent with the original number, work through the diagnosis in order. First, check whether the environment sync actually reproduced the exact locked versions. Second, check whether the metadata file actually has all three randomness layers — a missing one is the single most common cause of a near-miss. Third, confirm the checked-out commit is exactly the tagged one, not a descendant with unrecorded changes. Only after ruling out those three do you consider a genuine silent SDK break.

A reproducible experiment record is also the foundation Chapter 5 needs for resource estimation and profiling — estimating cost or runtime is only meaningful against the same pinned, recorded configuration you'd actually deploy. Next lesson starts that chapter: profiling a quantum-classical hybrid program, where classical time and quantum time are two completely different costs.
